questions.q: How does inference-time quantization differ in goal from QLoRA's training-time quantization covered in Lesson 26?
options: There is no difference; they are the same technique with the same goal
QLoRA quantizes a frozen base model so it fits in memory while fine-tuning an adapter, while inference quantization compresses a finished model to reduce serving memory and improve latency/throughput
Inference quantization only applies to the tokenizer, not the model weights
QLoRA is used only at serving time, never during training
questions.explain: QLoRA's quantization goal is enabling fine-tuning under memory constraints with a frozen quantized base. Inference quantization's goal is compressing a completed model to reduce serving memory footprint and cost.

questions.q: Why does quantizing a model's weights to 4-bit often improve decode throughput, not just save memory?
options: Because decode is compute-bound, and fewer bits means fewer floating point operations per token
Because decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, so moving fewer bytes per weight during each decode step can directly reduce the time spent moving data
Because quantization eliminates the need for a KV cache
Because 4-bit weights automatically increase the model's context length
questions.explain: As established in the KV cache lesson, decode is memory-bandwidth-bound. Since quantized weights require moving fewer bytes, memory-bandwidth-bound decode can run faster, not just more memory-efficiently.

questions.q: What distinguishes GPTQ and AWQ from naive round-to-nearest (RTN) quantization?
options: GPTQ and AWQ both use a small calibration dataset to measure which weights' precision loss actually hurts outputs, and allocate precision accordingly, rather than rounding every weight the same way
RTN requires a calibration dataset while GPTQ and AWQ do not
GPTQ and AWQ can only be used during pretraining, not after a model is finished
There is no meaningful difference between RTN and calibration-based methods
questions.explain: GPTQ solves a per-layer least-squares problem using calibration data to minimize rounding error, and AWQ specifically protects activation-salient weights. Both outperform naive RTN at the same bit width because they target precision where it matters most.

questions.q: What specifically does AWQ (Activation-aware Weight Quantization) protect?
options: It protects the tokenizer's vocabulary from being modified
It protects the subset of weights that activations reveal to be most salient to the model's output, quantizing the remaining weights more aggressively
It protects the optimizer state during a fine-tuning run
It protects all weights equally, with no differentiation
questions.explain: AWQ uses activation statistics to identify which weights matter most to model outputs and preserves their precision more carefully, while quantizing less-salient weights more aggressively.

questions.q: What practice does this lesson recommend before shipping a quantized model to production?
options: Trust the memory and latency improvements alone as sufficient evidence the model is ready
Re-run the same evaluation set used on the full-precision checkpoint and examine the accuracy delta before deciding the quantization level is acceptable for the use case
Skip evaluation since quantization never affects accuracy
Only evaluate quantized models on throughput benchmarks, never on task accuracy
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly ties back to Chapter 7's evaluation discipline: never ship a quantized model on memory/latency numbers alone -- re-run the same eval set and look at the accuracy delta before deciding a quantization level is acceptable.
